title: Feedback-driven load shedding with model-aware degradation
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Background: We need a robust, explainable load-shedding layer that keeps Redwood SLOs (99th percentile tail latency targets and error rate <0.5%) during multi-region spikes and partial outages. Existing approaches (static priority queues + hard drops) either cause high variability for critical tenants or aggressive error rates for low-priority workloads.

Goal: Design and implement a feedback-driven admission controller that combines lightweight per-tenant prioritization, probabilistic admission decisions, and model-aware graceful degradation modes. The controller should: (1) respect per-tenant SLAs/SLOs, (2) operate consistently across regions with a centralized policy plane + local fast-path, (3) integrate with circuit breakers for downstream dependencies, and (4) provide observability and safety rails for rollouts.

Key components: 
- Telemetry-driven controller: a control loop that consumes token-level latency and throughput metrics, queue lengths, and KV-cache hit rates to compute dynamic admission targets. The loop runs at 1s control intervals with exponential smoothing.
- Probabilistic admission: when a queue is oversubscribed, instead of deterministic eviction we apply a tenant-weighted drop probability derived from SLO slack and recent error trends. This reduces synchronized drops and smooths tail latency.
- Rank-aware priority lanes: requests are assigned a priority score using: tenant priority, request cost estimate (expected token count * model cost factor), and recent quality sensitivity from our evals. Scores map to lanes (express, normal, best-effort) with lane-specific target concurrency.
- Model-aware degradation modes: define degradations that are semantically meaningful per request class: a) model fallback to faster quantized variant, b) prefix trimming (drop non-essential context), c) delayed completion (return truncated partial answer with structured hint), d) opportunistic cache replay (serve cached continuation). Each mode has a quantified expected latency and quality delta.
- Circuit breaker integration: per-region and per-tenant breakers that trip on sustained high queueing or backend failure rates. Breakers trigger fallback modes and escalate to probabilistic shedding if recovery doesn't occur.
- Multi-region coordination: policy plane stores global tenant priorities and maximum tolerated failure domains. Local controllers pull policies and publish anonymized health signals (PSI: percentile stabilized indicators) to the plane for cross-region decisions and cold-start ramps.

Metrics and SLOs to monitor: 
- SLOs: p99 latency < target (tenant-specific), success rate > 99.5% for high-tier tenants.
- Control signals: admission_accept_rate, lane_concurrency, drop_probability, fallback_usage_rate, quality_regressions_by_prompt_set.
- Safety monitors: sudden rise in fallback_usage_rate or quality_regressions triggers automatic rollback.

Design tradeoffs: 
- Local fast-path vs centralized decisioning: local controllers must act within 10ms of admission decision to avoid extra latency, so heavy ML policies live in the policy plane and are compiled to lightweight decision tables for the fast-path.
- Deterministic fairness vs stochastic smoothing: probabilistic admission reduces worst-case synchronized evictions but can increase per-request uncertainty — mitigate by biasing probability by SLO slack and recent errors.
- Quality vs latency: some degradations (trimming) are cheap but risky for semantic correctness; model fallback preserves semantics more often but at higher cost. We prefer conservative quality-preserving fallbacks for P0/P1 tenants.

Implementation plan: 
1) Spec and policy DSL (this ticket) — define the scoring function, degradation taxonomy, and rollout knobs. Link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/REL/Feedback+Load+Shedding+Spec
2) Local controller runtime changes — implement probabilistic admission path and lanes; add lightweight per-request cost estimator.
3) Policy plane additions — store tenant SLO targets, lane caps, and degradation permissions; expose API for Console.
4) Circuit breaker hooks — integrate with existing breaker library and add rollback triggers.
5) Observability & alerts — dashboards (per-tenant), SLO burn-rate, and canary rollout telemetry.
6) Experimentation — AB test on 10% traffic for 2 weeks using a shadow mode that computes decisions without enforcing them.

Rollout plan: shadow -> canary (5%) -> ramp (25% -> 50%) -> global. Safety gates: rollback on >5% increase in high-tier error rate or >10% drop in eval quality for tracked prompt sets.

Open questions: 
- Should we persist per-tenant moving averages in primary DB or keep in-memory with periodic reconciliation? (proposal: keep in-memory for speed, persist daily snapshots for debugging)
- How to quantify quality delta: continue using our prompt-set based regression tests; add synthetic utility score per prompt.

Acceptance criteria: 
- New admission path passes unit/integration tests and benchmarked to add <0.5ms median overhead on request path.
- Shadow mode matches production telemetry within 5% for control signals.
- Canary demonstrates maintained p99 latency and no regression in tracked prompt sets for P1 tenants.

Related artifacts: GitHub PR prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3147, Confluence spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/REL/Feedback+Load+Shedding+Spec, eval dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/ls/feedback-shedding
